title: japans pm has new ally foreign yield hogs 2026 09 10
author: Jon Sindreu
text:
LONDON, Sept 10 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Economists such as the Brookings Institution's Robin Brooks have popularised the idea
, opens new tab
 that Japanese bond yields are soaring because global investors fear a debt crisis, triggered by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's ​largesse and public debt near 200% of GDP. Some Wall Street strategists argue that the only way out is Japan ‌Inc selling part of its $5.3 trillion
, opens new tab
 — 120% of GDP — in foreign portfolio assets. Yet reality sits uneasily with those narratives: supposedly flighty foreign capital, not domestic money managers, are the ones happily snapping up Japanese sovereign paper.
For years, Japan has been watched for clues about whether chickens will come home to roost for vastly indebted developed ​economies. Despite recent energy crises rocking the world, the Bank of Japan has resisted raising interest rates too quickly, while Takaichi ​has pushed forward with a 370 trillion yen ($2.41 trillion) investment splurge.
To be sure, currency markets don't like her plans. ⁠The yen, historically weak, has fallen 4% over the past year, which has lifted inflation and bond yields by making imports more expensive. ​Tokyo's answer has been to seek support from Trump administration allies to prop up the currency, with mixed success. Earlier this week, the yen rebounded and ​10-year bond yields eased, but this was the result of the BOJ signalling that it will tighten monetary policy next week. Overall, Takaichi's promise to simultaneously deliver fiscal-led growth, less inflation and lower interest rates seems hard to square.
Yet that isn't deterring international investors, who are displaying little fear of a sovereign debt crisis. Over the ​past six months, foreigners bought a net 17.9 trillion yen ($116.51 billion) of Japanese fixed-income securities, including 3.4 trillion yen in August. Last week, Norway's ​mammoth $2.2 trillion wealth fund proposed
, opens new tab
 that Japanese sovereign bonds become 7.4% of its developed-market debt allocations, up from 4.6%. This comes alongside a two-year-long "Buy Japan" equity trade, which ‌seems ⁠to be broadening beyond currency-sensitive exporters.
Conversely, Japanese investors aren't yet selling foreign assets at scale. The Government Pension Investment Fund has not yet given any suggestion it plans to tilt its $2.1 trillion portfolio further towards domestic assets, despite speculation surrounding its management committee meeting last month.
A lot of the attraction for American and European investors is that they can buy 10-year Japanese bonds and hedge the currency risk with rolling three-month forward contracts. Because ​purchasers get paid to swap yen ​for pounds, euros or dollars, western ⁠investors can get an up to one percentage point yield pickup over their own government paper from this trade, according to Breakingviews calculations.
Unfortunately for Takaichi, this means foreign money alone won't fix her yen problem. But ​for now, it suggests she needn't go to bed fearing an imminent debt crisis.
